newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota profits surge, but slower growth seen ahead.
newsitem.headline: Toyota profits surge, but slower growth seen ahead.

text.p: Japan's top carmaker Toyota Motor Corp on Wednesday announced a hefty increase of more than 80 percent in parent profits during last business year, fuelled mainly by the weak yen and a cost-cutting drive.
The company forecast only marginal gains for this year, however, showing much more caution than financial analysts and using calculations based on a dollar/yen rate identical to last year's.
"Its estimates are conservative," said Seiji Sugiura, an analyst at Nomura Securities Co Ltd's research unit. "It is likely to revise its forecast upward later this year."
Toyota said it expected its parent profit to rise to 630 billion yen ($5.57 billion) in fiscal 1997/98, which began on April 1, barely above its result for the prior year.
For fiscal 1996/97, Toyota recorded a parent current profit of 620.41 billion yen ($5.49 billion), up 82.1 percent from the year ago and its third largest annual current profit on record.
"The weak yen boosted our parent operating income by 240 billion yen ($2.12 billion) and cost-cutting efforts pushed it up by 110 billion yen ($973 million)," a Toyota spokesman said.
Its 1996/97 parent sales were up 14.4 percent to 9.10 trillion yen ($80.5 billion), also a record.

Toyota's group net profit in the year to March 1997 rose 50.2 percent to 385.92 billion yen ($3.41 billion), its fourth largest yearly profit on record. The company did not give a forecast for group net profits in fiscal 1997/98.
Net profit is equal to current profit, which is pre-tax, minus taxes and extraordinary profits and losses.
The company's 1996/97 group sales rose 14.2 percent to a record 12.24 trillion yen ($108 billion).
The company expected its domestic sales growth to slow markedly this year, however, after healthy growth last year as consumers rushed to buy big-ticket items ahead of a sales tax increase.

Toyota vehicle sales worldwide grew 9.9 percent in 1996/97 to 4,560 million units, Toyota said, with sales in Japan, the carmaker's largest market, rising 7.7 percent while overseas sales increased 12.1 percent.
But the company forecast a scant 0.4 percent growth in its domestic sales to 2.24 million units this year.

"Domestic orders are weak, but we are not pessimistic as we plan to launch several new models this year and Japan has latent replacement demand," Toyota vice chairman Iwao Isomura told a news conference on Wednesday.
Isomura estimated Japan's overall domestic vehicle demand excluding 660 cc minivehicles at 5.40 million units in 1997/98, down from 5.56 million units in 1996/97.
Toyota owed last year's surge in profits largely to the weaker yen against the dollar, and some analysts said its earnings remained vulnerable to future exchange rate fluctuations.

The dollar/yen rate averaged 112 yen to the dollar in 1996/97, about 14 percent lower than a year earlier. A weak yen makes Japanese firms' products more competitive in overseas markets and boosts the yen value of sales in foreign currencies.
Toyota used a dollar/yen rate of 112 yen in calculating its earnings estimates for 1997/98 as well.
Isomura said a dollar/yen rate of 110 to 120 yen was best for his company. "Steep fluctuations are the worst thing. We want the exchange rate to remain between 110 and 120 yen," he said.
A one yen gain in the dollar against the yen translates into an extra 15 billion yen ($132 million) annually for Toyota in operating profits, he said.

Ahead of Toyota's earnings announcement, which came after the market's close, shares in the carmaker and other Japanese exporters fell on the Tokyo bourse due to the yen's renewed strength. Toyota shares ended down 100 yen at 3,480.
The dollar took a nosedive on Tuesday to less than 112 yen, its weakest level since December, although it edged back up above 114 yen in late Tokyo trading on Wednesday.
"At a dollar rate below 115 yen we cannot neglect the possible impact on the company's earnings," said Masanobu Kaizu, a strategist at Nomura Securities Co's research unit.
Rival automaker Honda Motor Co Ltd also announced a jump in profits this week, with group net profit more than tripling in the last business year due to the weaker yen. (1$=113)
